knowledge_base.response: Watering frequency depends on crop root depth and soil drainage. For solanaceous crops (tomatoes, potatoes, peppers), provide 1.5–2 inches (35–50 mm) of water per week, watering deeply at the root zone early in the morning. Allow the top 2 inches of soil to dry slightly between waterings to prevent root suffocation and Pythium root rot. For houseplants and succulents, use the soak-and-dry method, watering only when the top 50% of the potting medium is dry. (Source: PLLaMa Plant Science Corpus / Agronomy Journal)

Crops like tomatoes, corn, peppers, and potatoes require full sunlight (6–8+ hours of direct irradiance daily) for optimal photosynthesis and fruit set. Leafy greens (spinach, lettuce) and herbs tolerate partial shade (3–5 hours). For indoor botanicals (ficus, snake plant, pothos), provide bright indirect sunlight (10,000–20,000 lux) and avoid harsh direct window glare which causes foliar scorch. (Source: PLLaMa / Trends in Plant Science)

Optimal N-P-K nutrition follows crop phenological stages: during early vegetative growth, use a balanced or nitrogen-leaning ratio (NPK 10-10-10 or 12-6-6) to build foliar canopy. Upon flower bud initiation and fruit bulking, transition to high-phosphorus and high-potassium formulas (such as NPK 5-10-10 or 4-18-38 with calcium and magnesium) to support blossom retention and cellular integrity. Legumes (beans, peas) fix their own atmospheric nitrogen and require low-N formulations. (Source: PLLaMa / Plant and Soil Journal)

Blight management combines sanitation with targeted fungicides. For Early Blight (Alternaria solani), prune lower foliage touching the soil to eliminate soil-splash inocula, apply organic copper octanoate or Bacillus subtilis bioprotectants, and rotate crops for 3 years. For Late Blight (Phytophthora infestans), treat immediately with systemic fungicides (Mancozeb + Metalaxyl/Mefenoxam) and destroy severely blighted foliage to prevent sporangia dispersal. (Source: PLLaMa / Phytopathology Research)

Powdery mildew (Erysiphales) thrives in warm, dry weather with high relative humidity. Apply potassium bicarbonate (3 g/L), sulfur dust, or neem oil spray every 7–10 days on upper leaf surfaces. For Downy Mildew (Pseudoperonospora), which requires free leaf moisture, ensure wide row spacing for air circulation, use drip irrigation, and apply copper hydroxide or Dimethomorph. (Source: PLLaMa / European Journal of Plant Pathology)

PLLaMa (arXiv:2401.01600v1) is the first open-source Large Language Model specifically pretrained on 1.67 million scientific articles from 750 plant science journals (The Plant Cell, Plant Physiology, Phytopathology, etc.). Developed by researchers from UCSB, Lincoln, CAAS, and SLU, PLLaMa bridges the domain gap in botanical artificial intelligence, achieving high accuracy on specialized plant biology benchmarks. (GitHub: https://github.com/Xianjun-Yang/PLLaMa)

Blossom End Rot is a physiological disorder caused by localized calcium deficiency in expanding fruit tissues, usually triggered by erratic watering or root damage rather than a lack of soil calcium. Maintain uniform soil moisture with organic mulch and apply foliar calcium chloride or chelated calcium during rapid fruit expansion. (Source: PLLaMa / Horticulture Research)

Several common plants contain insoluble calcium oxalate crystals or cardiac glycosides that are toxic to pets (e.g., Lilies, Dieffenbachia, Philodendron, Foxglove). Non-toxic, pet-safe alternatives include Spider Plants, Boston Ferns, Calatheas, and African Violets. If pet ingestion occurs, contact a veterinary poison hotline immediately. (Source: Botanical Veterinary Science)
